transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Zoe Carter (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (CTO, PillarHealth), Jon Park (Head of Platform), Elena Ramirez (Security Architect)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood walked through multi-region routing and fallback policies for hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Customer concerns focused on SLA guarantees during region outages, deterministic fallback ordering, data residency implications of cross-region failover, and auditability for regulatory compliance. Next steps: pricing/SLA sheet, benchmark plan, private-deploy deep-dive.

Topics: fallback policies; active-active vs active-passive routing; warm standbys; routing priority by policy; data residency and KMS; observability and audit logs; canary/fallback behavior.

Transcript:
[00:00] Zoe (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining — I see Maya, Jon, Elena, and Marcus and I on the line. quick agenda: run through how we handle incidents and outages, fallback policies across hosted/dedicated/private, and SLA expectations. is that good?
[00:18] Maya (PillarHealth): yes that sounds right, we really need to understand how you avoid blackouts during region failures and what guarantees we can show to our risk team.
[00:29] Marcus (Redwood SE): great, i'll start with a high-level then dig into routing rules. our platform supports policy-based routing — you can do preference order, cost-based, and SLO-driven routing. in practice, for safety-critical apps you often set a strict priority list: region-a primary, region-b secondary, fallback to lower-tier model variant if GP capacity is constrained.
[00:52] Jon (PillarHealth): when you say model variant, do you mean a quantized variant or a smaller model? and does that happen automatically?
[01:03] Marcus: yes both — the runtime can degrade to a compatible model variant (for example 13B quantized) automatically. we recommend an explicit degradation policy in your rollout config: model-family -> variant-priority -> region-priority. there's also — apologies — automatic prefix/K-V cash, sorry K-V cache, that helps keep latency bounded for repeated prefixes so you don't always pay cold start.
[01:28] Elena (PillarHealth): pause — so if our primary region goes down and traffic is routed to another region, does that route cross data residency boundaries? our compliance team needs assurances on patient PII.
[01:41] Zoe: good question. we support region affinity policies and hard-residency constraints. you can define a policy that forbids cross-region failover for requests labeled as resident-data. in those cases we will either queue requests or return a controlled error depending on your tolerance.
[02:01] Maya: queueing isn't great for us at 99th percentiles; we need the system to stay available. can you do active-active between two private VPCs in different regions without egressing data to public cloud?
[02:16] Marcus: yes, for Redwood Private and Dedicated we support federated private endpoints. in active-active mode you can replicate the KV cache or warm standby models across the two sites. that said, replication introduces replication lag and you need to define RPO/RTO expectations. our suggested pattern for low-latency with residency is: active-active with intra-VPC peering (or transit), and use local KMS for keys.
[02:39] Jon: what about SLA? our procurement team will ask for specifics: what is the SLA for hosted versus dedicated? is there a different SLO for failover time?
[02:50] Zoe: hosted API SLA is our standard 99.9% uptime per region, with cross-region fallback best-effort. Dedicated gets a contractual SLA 99.95% with defined failover windows and a response/mitigation playbook. for Private deployments we provide platform support SLAs as part of the enterprise agreement — those are negotiable.
[03:10] Elena: 99.9% per region is fine but what happens when an entire region is down for, say, 45 minutes? do calls fail, or do they route to another region incurring potential residency violations?
[03:23] Marcus: that's where policies come in. you can choose between permissive fallback (route anywhere with compatible model) and strict residency fallback (return an error or fail closed). the default for healthcare customers is strict-residency-by-default unless you opt in to cross-region fallback and sign off on the data-flow implications.
[03:43] Maya: ok that helps. can you walk through a concrete example — like region-a loses capacity because of infra issue, what is the sequence?
[03:52] Marcus: sure. sequence of events — example:
[03:55] Marcus: (1) control plane detects degraded health in region-a via probes and metrics;
[04:01] Marcus: (2) if health < threshold we mark region-a degraded and start redirecting new sessions per routing policy;
[04:08] Marcus: (3) if routing policy allows cross-region, requests are routed to region-b to maintain availability;
[04:13] Marcus: (4) if model variants are used, we will switch to the next compatible variant with a short TTL to avoid cache misses;
[04:19] Marcus: (5) audit logs capture the region and model used for each request for compliance.
[04:23] Jon: and during that route, how do you preserve session context? our chat flows need KV cache across the failover.
[04:31] Marcus: we keep session affinity as long as the session is bound to the instance. for cross-region failover, we either replicate KV sync (async) or replay last N tokens from the client to rehydrate context. there is a small window where the chat may see a 50-200ms context rebuild.
[04:48] Speaker 1 (background noise): mm hmm
[04:52] Zoe: also worth flagging our sticky routing TTLs — you can control session stickiness so short-lived sessions don't bounce during transient spikes.
[05:00] Elena: what about observability? our auditors will want to see chain of custody for each request and proof that fallbacks happened.
[05:09] Marcus: we expose per-request metadata: region, instance-id, model-variant, latency, and an incident-tag if a fallback or degraded route was used. all of that feeds into the Console; and for Private deployments we can stream these logs to your SIEM or S3 bucket.
[05:24] Maya: is that immutable? like can we prove the logs weren't altered?
[05:28] Zoe: we support write-once object stores and can integrate with KMS/HSM signatures for log integrity. we also support export of signed audit bundles.
[05:36] Jon: ok on failures — do you do active draining or immediate cutoff? we've seen vendors that abruptly cut and that causes retries from clients to overload the fallback region.
[05:47] Marcus: we do staged draining: first new sessions are diverted, existing in-flight requests are allowed to finish, and we can also configure rate-limits on the destination region to avoid thundering herd. we also recommend client-side jittered retries and exponential backoff.
[06:05] Maya: does Redwood provide client-side SDKs that implement best-practice retries?
[06:10] Zoe: yes, our SDK has built-in retry policies that are Redwood-aware; they can read route hints and fall back to alternate endpoints gracefully.
[06:18] Elena: about DR tests — do you offer runbooks or run a joint failover drill? we'd prefer a rehearsal before we commit to Dedicated.
[06:27] Marcus: absolutely, we do runbooks and can do a joint tabletop and then a live failover drill with predefined success criteria. we log everything and provide a post-mortem report.
[06:36] Jon: on the networking side — if we do private deployment, what does cross-region peering look like? do you manage it or we manage it?
[06:44] Marcus: for Private we can support two models: customer-managed peering where your infra team sets up transit between sites, or Redwood-managed connectivity as part of the enterprise package. either way we support mutual TLS and you can bring your own IPSEC or AWS Transit Gateway.
[06:58] Maya: any suggestions on minimizing RTO when we need to start a failover — warm standby or active-active?
[07:05] Marcus: warm standby is easiest to manage and cost-efficient: you have a hot model loaded but no traffic until failover. active-active reduces failover time but increases inter-region replication cost. for low-latency needs we recommend active-active with local model weights and async KV replication.
[07:20] Zoe: worth noting from a cost perspective, Dedicated capacity can reserve GPU pools in multiple regions and give you pre-warmed capacity so failover is instantaneous within the reserved pool.
[07:31] Maya: if we reserve capacity in multiple regions, does Redwood bill double? we need to justify cost.
[07:37] Zoe: reserved capacity is priced per region; you pay for the committed pool. we do provide a burst model and brokerage to shift some load in emergencies to our hosted fleet at a different price. that's in the Dedicated pricing sheet.
[07:50] Jon: can you commit to a failover time in SLA, like 5 minutes to reroute?
[07:55] Zoe: we define failover SLAs in Dedicated contracts — typical wording is mean time to failover detection + mitigation within X minutes, where X depends on the configuration. for strict-residency configurations we often can't promise cross-region failover in the SLA unless we have signed residency waivers.
[08:13] Elena: what about degraded output quality — if you switch to smaller model variants, do you provide regression testing and alerting? we need to know if quality would drop below an approved threshold.
[08:24] Marcus: yes, Redwood Optimize ties model variant recommendations to eval sets. we can tie alerts to BLEU-like or application-specific metrics, and we can gate cross-region fallback on quality thresholds so if switching variants would reduce quality beyond your threshold we either block it or notify you.
[08:40] Maya: helpful. on incident tolerance, do you support canary fallbacks? like route 5% to the fallback region first? we want to avoid surprising behavior.
[08:50] Marcus: yes, there's canary routing and gradual ramping. policies can be time-based or load-based. you can configure percent-rollouts for failover and rollback automatically if error rates spike.
[09:01] Speaker 2 (Jon): is the rollback instant?
[09:04] Marcus: rollback is automatic if error rates exceed the configured threshold or you manually trigger it. logs and traces are preserved for audit.
[09:12] Zoe: quick pause: Elena — any specific regulatory constraints we should be aware of beyond residency and audit logs?
[09:19] Elena: encryption at rest and in transit — KMS integration, customer-managed keys, HSM for signing, SOC 2, ISO 27001 evidence. also we need longer retention for audit trails, like seven years.
[09:34] Zoe: we support BYOK (bring your own key) and HSM-backed signing; retention is configurable and we can set longer retention buckets for audit trails.
[09:43] Maya: ok this has been a lot. can we talk about failure modes — e.g., control plane outage vs data plane outage? how is each handled?
[09:53] Marcus: short answer: control plane failures primarily affect management operations (rollouts, config changes) but the data plane keeps serving if pre-provisioned. if control plane is down we rely on cached configs on nodes. data plane outages are mitigated by routing to other healthy data plane regions or to hosted fallback.
[10:10] Maya: so our apps would still get inference responses even if control plane is partially degraded?
[10:15] Marcus: yes, assuming you have pre-warmed capacity and the routing policy allows fallback.
[10:20] Jon: one more — do you support policy to prefer on-prem hardware (edge) for certain customers?
[10:27] Marcus: we do; on-prem nodes can be added to the routing fabric and given priority. that is common for regulated customers.
[10:33] Zoe: all right let's surface a couple of real-world tradeoffs you should be aware of, Maya: 1) strict residency = higher risk of temporary unavailability vs permissive fallback = availability but cross-region data flow, 2) active-active = lower RTO but higher cost and complexity, 3) model-variant fallback = cheaper and more available but potential quality drop.
[10:52] Maya: yep, that's the trade space. do you have any documented runbook examples?
[10:56] Marcus: yes — i can attach a DR-runbook template and a post-mortem checklist.
[11:02] Zoe: let's step through a putative timeline for procurement: you evaluate Dedicated, run a pilot with small reserved capacity in two regions, run DR drill, then expand. during pilot we'll provide a temporary SLA addendum.
[11:16] Jon: technical question — how do you detect region health? is it active probes or passive metrics?
[11:21] Marcus: both. we run active synthetic probes, passive latency/error signal aggregation, and cross-region heartbeat checks. we also ingest infra signals like GPU metrics and network errors.
[11:33] Elena: in the event of a partial outage, how granular are your fallback logs? can we get per-token metadata?
[11:40] Marcus: yes per-token metadata is available for debugging but note that's high-volume — usually we sample, and for audits we provide full request metadata tied to authentication tokens for a given window.
[11:53] Zoe: note for privacy-sensitive tokens we can hash or tokenize identifiers before storing.
[11:59] Maya: what's the expected maintenance window behavior? we need to schedule weekly patching without affecting SLAs.
[12:06] Zoe: maintenance windows are negotiated; Dedicated customers get scheduled maintenance notifications and we can coordinate to ensure capacity across regions during planned updates. maintenance is excluded from SLA calculations if notified in advance per contract terms.
[12:21] Jon: ok, curious — have you had multi-hour region outages before and how did Redwood handle them?
[12:28] Marcus: yes, we had a provider-level network event last year. we routed traffic using cross-region routing, invoked burst-to-hosted policy for some customers, and ran post-mortems. for Dedicated customers we offered temporary credits and helped with warm-up in target regions.
[12:45] Maya: thanks — can you send the post-mortem for that incident? it will help our risk team.
[12:49] Zoe: yes, i'll include the redacted post-mortem in the security pack.
[12:53] Elena: about the security pack — can you include SOC 2 type II report and a third-party penetration test?
[12:59] Zoe: yes, we'll include SOC 2, ISO attestation, pen-test summary, and the runbook.
[13:07] Marcus: back to routing — one more nuance: we support circuit-breaker style rules that cut traffic to a region if error rates exceed a limit and can gradually reintroduce traffic with canaries.
[13:19] Jon: that would help with the thundering herd problem.
[13:22] Marcus: exactly.
[13:24] Maya: are any of those controls exposed in the Console or API? we prefer API-first config.
[13:29] Zoe: both. the Console has safe defaults and templates; the API exposes routing policy resources and you can include them in infra as code.
[13:37] Jon: great. do you have metrics on typical failover latencies? ballpark numbers?
[13:42] Marcus: warm-standby failover is usually sub-60s for session routing; active-active is effectively instantaneous from the client's perspective (under 5-10ms added latency aside), and full cold starts (if you need to spin up new model instances) can be multiple minutes.
[13:58] Maya: that range is helpful. for our SLA ask we'll likely target a 2-minute detection+reroute for user-facing requests. is that reasonable?
[14:07] Zoe: for Dedicated with reserved warm capacity in region-b, yes we can agree to contractual detection + 2 minutes reroute. we'll draft language for procurement.
[14:16] Elena: will that require a double-reservation of GPU pools?
[14:20] Zoe: yes you'll pay for the reserved pool in both regions unless you allow Redwood-hosted burst as an alternative.
[14:27] Jon: cost question — is there an ability to autoscale the warm standby based on health signals?
[14:32] Marcus: autoscale is supported; warm standby scaling is constrained by model load times. we can auto-scale via pre-warmed model snapshots to reduce scale-up time.
[14:43] Maya: ok, i'm thinking about the procurement story and what our team will ask — can you provide a one-page summary that calls out the options and the tradeoffs?
[14:51] Zoe: yes, we'll do a 'resilience options' one-pager that lists strict residency, permissive fallback, active-active, warm-standby, cost implications, and suggested configs for healthcare workloads.
[14:59] Marcus: and i'll include sample routing YAML and a short benchmark plan for the pilot.
[15:06] Maya: excellent. last question for now — in the pilot, can we do a partial traffic shift to the Dedicated pool and keep the rest on hosted? we want to test both.
[15:15] Marcus: you can do hybrid routing — route a percentage to Dedicated and fall back to hosted only for overflow. that's a common pattern for pilots.
[15:25] Zoe: ok let's capture next steps and action items.
[15:28] Zoe: next steps recap: 1) Zoe to send SLA/pricing and security pack; 2) Marcus to send runbook, routing samples, and benchmark plan; 3) Maya to share sample payloads and QPS targets; 4) schedule private deployment deep-dive for 2025-03-26.
[15:45] Jon: sounds good.
[15:47] Elena: thanks, we'll review and follow up with specific questions.
[15:51] Maya: appreciate the thoroughness.
[15:53] Zoe: great — we'll get those docs over this week. thanks all.

End of transcript.
